notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Ecology is the study of relationships among organisms and between organisms and their environment.
  • The word ecology is derived from Greek oikos meaning house or habitat and logos meaning study.
  • Ernst Haeckel coined the term ecology in 1866.
  • Ecology operates at several levels, from individuals to the biosphere.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ecology → Organisms + Environment

Ernst Haeckel → Ecology → 1866

2. Levels of Ecological Organisation

Important levels are:

  • Organism
  • Population
  • Community
  • Ecosystem
  • Biome
  • Biosphere
📌 Memory

Organism → Population → Community → Ecosystem → Biome → Biosphere

3. Organism
  • An organism is an individual living entity.
  • Organismal ecology studies how an individual responds to its environment.
  • Physiological and behavioural adaptations help organisms survive environmental conditions.
4. Population
  • A population consists of individuals of the same species living in a particular area.
  • Members of a population can potentially interact and reproduce.
  • Population size changes through birth, death, immigration and emigration.
5. Community
  • A community consists of populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.
  • Community ecology studies interactions such as competition, predation and mutualism.
6. Ecosystem
  • An ecosystem consists of living organisms and the non-living environment interacting as a functional unit.
  • Ecosystems involve energy flow and nutrient cycling.
  • Ecosystems may be natural or artificial.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ecosystem = Biotic + Abiotic Components

7. Ecosystem Term
  • British ecologist Arthur G. Tansley introduced the term ecosystem in 1935.
📌 Must-Memorise

A.G. Tansley → Ecosystem → 1935

8. Biotic Components

Biotic components are living components.

They include:

  • Producers
  • Consumers
  • Decomposers
  • Detritivores
9. Abiotic Components

Abiotic components include:

  • Light
  • Temperature
  • Water
  • Air
  • Soil
  • Minerals
  • pH
  • Salinity
  • Humidity
10. Producers
  • Producers manufacture organic food from inorganic substances.
  • Green plants are the major terrestrial producers.
  • Algae and cyanobacteria are important aquatic producers.
  • Producers form the first trophic level.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

First Trophic Level → Producers

11. Autotrophs
  • Autotrophs manufacture their own organic food.
  • Photoautotrophs use light energy.
  • Chemoautotrophs obtain energy from chemical reactions.
  • Plants are primarily photoautotrophs.
12. Consumers

Consumers obtain energy by eating other organisms.

They include:

  • Primary consumers
  • Secondary consumers
  • Tertiary consumers
  • Omnivores
13. Primary Consumers
  • Primary consumers feed directly on producers.
  • Most are herbivores.
  • They occupy the second trophic level.
📌 Example

Grass → Deer

Deer → Primary consumer

14. Secondary Consumers
  • Secondary consumers feed mainly on primary consumers.
  • They commonly occupy the third trophic level.
15. Tertiary Consumers
  • Tertiary consumers feed on secondary consumers.
  • They may occur near the top of a food chain.
16. Decomposers
  • Decomposers break down dead organic matter.
  • Bacteria and fungi are major decomposers.
  • They convert complex organic substances into simpler compounds.
  • They recycle nutrients back into ecosystems.
📌 Must-Memorise

Major Decomposers → Bacteria + Fungi

17. Detritivores
  • Detritivores feed directly on dead organic material.
  • Earthworms are important detritivores.
  • Termites and some arthropods also process detritus.
  • Detritivores physically fragment organic matter.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Detritivore and decomposer are related but not identical terms.

18. Food Chain
  • A food chain represents a linear pathway of energy transfer.
  • Energy moves from producers to consumers.
  • Food chains usually contain only a limited number of trophic levels because energy is lost at every transfer.
19. Grazing Food Chain

A grazing food chain begins with living green plants.

Example:

Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Grazing Food Chain → Starts with Producer

20. Detritus Food Chain
  • A detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter.
  • Detritivores and decomposers process dead material.
  • Detritus pathways are particularly important in forests and soil ecosystems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Detritus Food Chain → Starts with Dead Organic Matter

21. Food Web
  • A food web consists of interconnected food chains.
  • Most organisms have more than one food source or predator.
  • Food webs better represent natural ecosystems than simple food chains.
22. Trophic Level
  • A trophic level is a feeding position within a food chain.
  • Producers occupy the first trophic level.
  • Herbivores usually occupy the second.
  • Primary carnivores occupy higher levels.
23. Energy Flow
  • Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight.
  • Producers convert light energy into chemical energy.
  • Energy flows through trophic levels.
  • Unlike nutrients, energy is not recycled.
  • Much energy eventually leaves the ecosystem as heat.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Energy → Unidirectional Flow

Nutrients → Cyclic Flow

24. Ten Percent Law
  • Raymond Lindeman formulated the ecological ten-percent concept.
  • On average, only a small fraction of energy at one trophic level becomes biomass available to the next.
  • The textbook approximation is about 10%.
📌 Must-Memorise

10% Law → Raymond Lindeman

25. Why Food Chains Are Short
  • Energy is lost at every trophic transfer.
  • Organisms use much energy for respiration, movement and metabolism.
  • Energy dissipates as heat.
  • Therefore, long food chains cannot support large populations at upper levels.
26. Ecological Pyramid

Ecological pyramids may represent:

  • Numbers
  • Biomass
  • Energy
27. Pyramid of Numbers
  • Pyramid of numbers shows number of organisms at each trophic level.
  • It may be upright or inverted.
  • A tree ecosystem can support many insects, producing an inverted or irregular numbers pyramid.
28. Pyramid of Biomass
  • Biomass pyramid shows living mass at each trophic level.
  • Terrestrial biomass pyramids are generally upright.
  • Aquatic biomass pyramids can be inverted because phytoplankton reproduce rapidly despite low standing biomass.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Biomass Pyramid → Can Be Inverted.

29. Pyramid of Energy
  • Energy pyramid shows energy flow through trophic levels.
  • It is always upright.
  • Energy decreases at every successive trophic level.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pyramid Always Upright → Energy Pyramid

30. Biomass
  • Biomass is the total mass of living organic material in a given area or trophic level.
  • It is often expressed as dry mass per unit area.
31. Primary Productivity
  • Primary productivity is the rate at which producers create organic matter.
  • Photosynthesis is the main basis of primary productivity.
  • It is measured per unit area per unit time.
32. Gross Primary Productivity
  • GPP stands for Gross Primary Productivity.
  • It is the total rate of photosynthetic production by producers.
33. Net Primary Productivity
  • NPP stands for Net Primary Productivity.
  • It is the energy or biomass remaining after plant respiration.
📌 Formula

NPP = GPP − R

where R = respiration loss.

📌 Must-Memorise

NPP = GPP − Respiration

34. Secondary Productivity
  • Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new biomass by consumers.
  • It depends on food consumed and assimilation efficiency.
35. Decomposition
  • Decomposition breaks down dead organic matter.
  • It releases inorganic nutrients back into the environment.
  • Major decomposers are fungi and bacteria.
36. Major Steps of Decomposition

Important processes include:

  • Fragmentation
  • Leaching
  • Catabolism
  • Humification
  • Mineralisation
37. Fragmentation
  • Detritivores break large pieces of dead material into smaller particles.
  • Earthworms contribute strongly to fragmentation.
38. Leaching
  • Water dissolves soluble nutrients from dead material and carries them into soil.
39. Catabolism
  • Bacterial and fungal enzymes break complex organic compounds into simpler substances.
40. Humification
  • Humification forms dark, relatively resistant organic material called humus.
  • Humus decomposes slowly.
  • It improves soil properties.
41. Mineralisation
  • Microorganisms convert organic nutrients into inorganic mineral forms.
  • These nutrients can again become available to plants.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mineralisation → Organic Nutrients → Inorganic Nutrients

42. Biogeochemical Cycles

Biogeochemical cycles move elements between living organisms and the physical environment.

Important cycles include:

  • Water cycle
  • Carbon cycle
  • Nitrogen cycle
  • Phosphorus cycle
  • Sulfur cycle
43. Water Cycle

Major processes include:

  • Evaporation
  • Transpiration
  • Condensation
  • Precipitation
  • Infiltration
  • Runoff
44. Evapotranspiration
  • Evapotranspiration is the combined loss of water by evaporation and plant transpiration.
45. Carbon Cycle
  • Carbon circulates through atmosphere, organisms, oceans, soils and rocks.
  • Plants absorb atmospheric CO₂ during photosynthesis.
  • Respiration returns CO₂.
  • Decomposition releases carbon.
  • Fossil-fuel combustion adds stored carbon to the atmosphere.
46. Major Carbon Sinks

Important carbon reservoirs/sinks include:

  • Oceans.
  • Forests.
  • Soils.
  • Sedimentary rocks.
  • A carbon sink absorbs more carbon than it releases over a period.
47. Carbon Sequestration
  • Carbon sequestration means long-term capture and storage of carbon.
  • Forests and soils naturally store carbon.
  • Geological storage can also be used technologically.
48. Nitrogen Cycle

Major processes include:

  • Nitrogen fixation
  • Ammonification
  • Nitrification
  • Assimilation
  • Denitrification
49. Nitrogen Fixation
  • Atmospheric nitrogen is N₂.
  • Most plants cannot directly use N₂.
  • Nitrogen-fixing organisms convert N₂ into ammonia or related usable forms.
50. Biological Nitrogen Fixers

Important examples:

  • Rhizobium
  • Azotobacter
  • Azospirillum
  • Anabaena
  • Nostoc
51. Ammonification
  • Organic nitrogen from dead organisms and wastes is converted into ammonia/ammonium by decomposers.
📌 Memory

Organic N → NH₃/NH₄⁺

52. Nitrification

Classical textbook sequence:

NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻

  • Nitrosomonas is associated with ammonium-to-nitrite oxidation.
  • Nitrobacter is traditionally associated with nitrite-to-nitrate oxidation.
53. Denitrification
  • Denitrifying microorganisms convert nitrate into gaseous nitrogen forms.
  • This returns nitrogen to the atmosphere.
  • Pseudomonas is a commonly cited denitrifier.
54. Phosphorus Cycle
  • Phosphorus circulates mainly through rocks, soil, water and organisms.
  • Weathering releases phosphate.
  • Plants absorb phosphate from soil.
  • Animals obtain phosphorus through food.
  • Decomposition returns phosphorus.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Phosphorus Cycle → Major Sedimentary Cycle

55. Special Feature of Phosphorus Cycle
  • The phosphorus cycle has no major atmospheric gaseous phase.
  • This distinguishes it from carbon and nitrogen cycles.
📌 Must-Memorise

Phosphorus Cycle → No Significant Gaseous Phase

56. Habitat
  • Habitat is the physical place where an organism lives.
  • A habitat provides food, water, shelter and suitable environmental conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Habitat → Where It Lives

57. Ecological Niche
  • A niche describes the functional role and ecological requirements of a species.
  • It includes food use, habitat use, interactions and environmental tolerances.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Habitat → Address

Niche → Role/Profession

58. Ecotone
  • An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems or communities.
  • Species from both adjacent communities may occur there.
  • Ecotones can show high species diversity.
59. Edge Effect
  • Edge effect refers to changes in population or community structure at ecosystem boundaries.
  • Some species thrive particularly at edges.
60. Biome
  • A biome is a large ecological region characterised mainly by climate and dominant vegetation.
  • Major terrestrial biomes include deserts, grasslands, forests and tundra.
61. Tundra
  • Tundra occurs in very cold regions.
  • Permafrost is common.
  • Vegetation is low-growing.
  • Mosses and lichens are prominent.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tundra → Permafrost

62. Desert
  • Deserts have very low precipitation.
  • Plants and animals show water-conservation adaptations.
  • Xerophytes are plants adapted to dry conditions.
63. Xerophytes

Common xerophytic adaptations include:

  • Reduced leaves/spines
  • Thick cuticle
  • Succulent water-storage tissues
  • Sunken stomata
  • Extensive roots
64. Grasslands
  • Grasslands are dominated by grasses.
  • Fire and grazing help maintain many grasslands.
  • Savannas are tropical grasslands with scattered trees.
65. Tropical Rainforest
  • Tropical rainforests occur in warm, high-rainfall regions.
  • They have very high biodiversity.
  • Vegetation forms multiple layers.
  • Nutrient cycling is rapid.
66. Aquatic Ecosystems

Major categories include:

  • Freshwater
  • Marine
  • Estuarine
67. Lentic Ecosystem
  • Lentic ecosystems contain standing water.
  • Examples include lakes and ponds.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lentic → Standing Water

68. Lotic Ecosystem
  • Lotic ecosystems contain flowing water.
  • Examples include rivers and streams.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lotic → Flowing Water

69. Estuary
  • An estuary is where freshwater mixes with seawater.
  • Estuarine water is generally brackish.
  • Estuaries are highly productive ecosystems.
  • They serve as nurseries for many aquatic organisms.
70. Wetlands
  • Wetlands are areas where water strongly influences soil and biological conditions.
  • They include marshes, swamps and some shallow-water habitats.
  • Wetlands control floods, recharge groundwater, store carbon and support biodiversity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Wetlands → Natural Water Filters + Flood Buffers

71. Mangroves
  • Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees and shrubs of tropical and subtropical coasts.
  • They occur in intertidal areas.
  • They protect shorelines.
  • They provide nursery habitat for fish and crustaceans.
  • Many species possess specialised roots.
72. Pneumatophores
  • Pneumatophores are specialised aerial roots used for gas exchange in waterlogged soils.
  • They are common in several mangrove species.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mangrove Respiratory Roots → Pneumatophores

73. Coral Reefs
  • Coral reefs are formed mainly by reef-building corals.
  • Corals are cnidarian animals.
  • Reef-building corals secrete calcium-carbonate skeletons.
  • Coral reefs support extremely high marine biodiversity.
74. Zooxanthellae
  • Reef-building corals commonly contain symbiotic photosynthetic dinoflagellates.
  • These are traditionally called zooxanthellae.
  • They provide organic nutrients to corals.
75. Coral Bleaching
  • Coral bleaching occurs when stressed corals lose or expel their symbiotic algae or their pigments decline.
  • High sea temperatures are a major cause of mass bleaching.
  • Prolonged bleaching can cause coral mortality.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Coral Bleaching → Heat Stress + Loss of Symbiotic Algae

76. Population Density
  • Population density is the number of individuals per unit area or volume.
  • Population density changes over time.
77. Natality
  • Natality means birth rate.
  • Births increase population size.
78. Mortality
  • Mortality means death rate.
  • Deaths decrease population size.
79. Immigration
  • Immigration is movement of individuals into a population.
  • It increases population size.
80. Emigration
  • Emigration is movement of individuals out of a population.
  • It decreases population size.
📌 Memory

Population Increase → Birth + Immigration

Population Decrease → Death + Emigration

81. Population Growth

Two basic models are:

  • Exponential growth
  • Logistic growth
82. Exponential Growth
  • Exponential growth occurs under ideal conditions with abundant resources.
  • It produces a J-shaped growth curve.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Exponential Growth → J Curve

83. Logistic Growth
  • Logistic growth occurs when resources become limiting.
  • Growth slows as population approaches carrying capacity.
  • It produces an S-shaped or sigmoid curve.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Logistic Growth → S Curve

84. Carrying Capacity
  • Carrying capacity is the maximum population size an environment can support sustainably under particular conditions.
  • It is commonly represented by K.
📌 Must-Memorise

Carrying Capacity → K

85. Age Structure

Population age groups are commonly:

  • Pre-reproductive.
  • Reproductive.
  • Post-reproductive.
  • Age structure helps predict future population trends.
86. Expanding Population Pyramid
  • Broad base.
  • High proportion of young individuals.
  • Indicates potential rapid population growth.
87. Stable Population Pyramid
  • Pre-reproductive and reproductive groups are relatively balanced.
  • Population size remains comparatively stable.
88. Declining Population Pyramid
  • Narrow base.
  • Lower proportion of young individuals.
  • Population may decline over time.
89. Species Interactions

Major ecological interactions include:

  • Mutualism
  • Commensalism
  • Parasitism
  • Predation
  • Competition
  • Amensalism
90. Mutualism
  • Both species benefit.
  • Examples include mycorrhiza and many pollinator-plant relationships.
📌 Symbol

+/+

91. Lichen
  • Lichen is an association between fungus and a photosynthetic alga or cyanobacterium.
  • It is a classic mutualistic association.
92. Mycorrhiza
  • Mycorrhiza is an association between fungus and plant roots.
  • Fungus improves mineral and water uptake.
  • Plant supplies carbohydrates.
93. Commensalism
  • One species benefits.
  • The other is neither significantly helped nor harmed.
📌 Symbol

+/0

Example:

  • Epiphytic orchids growing on trees in traditional textbook examples.
94. Parasitism
  • Parasite benefits.
  • Host is harmed.
📌 Symbol

+/−

Examples:

  • Tapeworm in humans.
  • Cuscuta on plants.
  • Plasmodium in humans.
95. Predation
  • Predator kills and consumes prey.
  • Predation helps regulate prey populations.
  • Predators can influence community diversity.
📌 Symbol

+/−

96. Competition
  • Competition occurs when organisms use a limited resource.
  • Both competitors may experience reduced fitness.
📌 Symbol

−/−

97. Competitive Exclusion Principle
  • G.F. Gause proposed the competitive exclusion principle.
  • Two species with identical ecological requirements cannot coexist indefinitely when a limiting resource is scarce.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gause → Competitive Exclusion Principle

98. Resource Partitioning
  • Competing species can coexist by using resources differently.
  • Differences may involve time, location or food type.
  • This reduces direct competition.
99. Amensalism
  • One species is harmed while the other is essentially unaffected.
📌 Symbol

−/0

  • Antibiotic production by some microorganisms is a commonly cited example.
100. Ecological Succession
  • Succession is gradual change in community composition over time.
  • Pioneer species colonise first.
  • Communities change until a relatively stable mature community develops.
101. Primary Succession
  • Primary succession begins on a surface without developed soil.
  • Examples include newly exposed bare rock or fresh volcanic material.
  • It proceeds slowly because soil must develop.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Primary Succession → Starts Without Soil

102. Pioneer Species
  • Lichens are common pioneer organisms on bare rock.
  • They contribute to rock weathering and early soil formation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bare Rock Pioneer → Lichens

103. Secondary Succession
  • Secondary succession occurs where a previous community was disturbed but soil remains.
  • Examples include abandoned farmland and areas recovering after some fires.
  • It is generally faster than primary succession.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Secondary Succession → Soil Already Present

104. Hydrarch Succession
  • Hydrarch or hydrosere succession begins in aquatic or very wet environments.
  • Communities gradually become less aquatic as sediment and organic matter accumulate.
105. Xerarch Succession
  • Xerarch succession begins in dry habitats.
  • Bare-rock succession is a common example.
106. Biodiversity

Biodiversity includes variation at three main levels:

  • Genetic diversity
  • Species diversity
  • Ecosystem diversity
📌 Must-Memorise

Biodiversity → Genetic + Species + Ecosystem

107. Genetic Diversity
  • Genetic diversity means variation in genes within a species.
  • It allows populations to respond to environmental change.
  • Crop varieties and livestock breeds demonstrate genetic diversity.
108. Species Diversity
  • Species diversity reflects variety and relative abundance of species.
  • It includes species richness and evenness.
109. Species Richness
  • Species richness is the number of species in a given area.
110. Species Evenness
  • Species evenness describes how evenly individuals are distributed among species.
111. Ecosystem Diversity
  • Ecosystem diversity refers to variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes.
112. Alpha Diversity
  • Alpha diversity refers to diversity within a particular habitat or local community.
113. Beta Diversity
  • Beta diversity describes change in species composition between habitats.
114. Gamma Diversity
  • Gamma diversity refers to overall diversity across a large landscape or region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Alpha → Within Habitat

Beta → Between Habitats

Gamma → Regional

115. Endemic Species
  • An endemic species naturally occurs only in a particular geographic area.
  • Endemic species can be especially vulnerable to habitat destruction because of their limited distribution.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Endemic → Restricted Geographic Distribution

116. Exotic Species
  • Exotic or alien species occur outside their natural geographic range because of human activity.
  • Not every exotic species becomes harmful.
117. Invasive Alien Species
  • An invasive alien species spreads outside its native range and causes ecological, economic or health damage.
  • Invasives can outcompete native species and alter ecosystems.
118. Important Invasive Plants in India

Common examples include:

  • Lantana camara
  • Parthenium hysterophorus
  • Eichhornia crassipes
  • Prosopis juliflora
119. Water Hyacinth
  • Eichhornia crassipes is water hyacinth.
  • It is an invasive aquatic plant.
  • Dense growth blocks waterways and reduces oxygen and light.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Water Hyacinth → Eichhornia crassipes

120. Parthenium
  • Parthenium hysterophorus is an invasive weed.
  • It is commonly called congress grass.
  • It can cause allergies and suppress native vegetation.
121. Keystone Species
  • A keystone species has an ecological impact disproportionately large compared with its abundance.
  • Removing it can cause major community changes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Keystone Species → Disproportionately Large Ecological Role

122. Flagship Species
  • Flagship species are charismatic organisms used to generate public support for conservation.
  • Tiger and elephant are common Indian examples.
123. Umbrella Species
  • Protecting an umbrella species requires conserving a large habitat.
  • This indirectly protects many other organisms within that habitat.
124. Indicator Species
  • Indicator species provide information about environmental conditions.
  • Lichens can indicate air quality.
  • Some aquatic organisms indicate water quality.
125. Biodiversity Hotspot
  • A biodiversity hotspot has exceptionally high endemism and faces severe habitat loss.
  • Norman Myers developed the hotspot concept.
  • Hotspots are priorities for conservation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Biodiversity Hotspot Concept → Norman Myers

126. Biodiversity Hotspots Associated with India

India includes parts of four recognised global biodiversity hotspots:

  • Himalaya
  • Indo-Burma
  • Western Ghats–Sri Lanka
  • Sundaland
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Indian part of Sundaland hotspot → Nicobar Islands.

127. Western Ghats
  • Western Ghats are exceptionally rich in endemic plants and animals.
  • They form part of the Western Ghats–Sri Lanka biodiversity hotspot.
  • Parts of Tamil Nadu lie within the Western Ghats.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tamil Nadu Biodiversity → Western Ghats Hotspot

128. Threats to Biodiversity

Major threats include:

  • Habitat destruction
  • Habitat fragmentation
  • Overexploitation
  • Invasive species
  • Pollution
  • Climate change
  • Illegal wildlife trade
129. Habitat Fragmentation
  • Fragmentation divides a continuous habitat into smaller isolated patches.
  • It reduces movement and gene flow.
  • It increases edge effects.
  • Small isolated populations are more vulnerable to extinction.
130. Overexploitation
  • Overexploitation occurs when organisms are harvested faster than populations can recover.
  • Hunting, overfishing and excessive timber extraction can cause population decline.
131. Extinction
  • Extinction is permanent disappearance of a species.
  • Local extinction from one region is called extirpation.
  • Human activity has accelerated extinction rates.
132. In-Situ Conservation
  • In-situ conservation protects species within their natural habitats.

Examples include:

  • National parks
  • Wildlife sanctuaries
  • Biosphere reserves
  • Community-conserved habitats
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

In-Situ → In Natural Habitat

133. Ex-Situ Conservation
  • Ex-situ conservation protects organisms outside their natural habitats.

Examples include:

  • Zoos
  • Botanical gardens
  • Seed banks
  • Gene banks
  • Captive breeding
  • Cryopreservation
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ex-Situ → Outside Natural Habitat

134. National Park
  • A national park is established for protection of ecosystems and wildlife.
  • Human activities are more strictly restricted than in many multi-use landscapes.
  • National parks are important in-situ conservation areas.
135. Wildlife Sanctuary
  • Wildlife sanctuaries protect wild animals and their habitats.
  • Certain regulated human activities may be allowed according to legal provisions.
  • They are in-situ conservation areas.
136. Biosphere Reserve
  • Biosphere reserves combine biodiversity conservation with sustainable use and research.
  • They are generally organised into zones.

Major zones are:

  • Core
  • Buffer
  • Transition
📌 Must-Memorise

Biosphere Reserve → Core + Buffer + Transition

137. Core Zone
  • Core zone receives the highest level of ecosystem protection.
  • Conservation and research are major activities.
138. Buffer Zone
  • Buffer surrounds or adjoins the core.
  • Research, education and compatible activities may occur.
139. Transition Zone
  • Transition zone accommodates sustainable human activities and settlements.
140. Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve
  • Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve lies across Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka.
  • It was India's first biosphere reserve, established in 1986.
  • It includes important Western Ghats ecosystems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

India's First Biosphere Reserve → Nilgiri → 1986

141. Gulf of Mannar
  • Gulf of Mannar in Tamil Nadu supports coral reefs, seagrass beds, mangroves and marine biodiversity.
  • It is an important marine conservation region.
  • Dugongs occur in this broader coastal ecosystem.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tamil Nadu Marine Biodiversity → Gulf of Mannar

142. Sacred Groves
  • Sacred groves are forest patches traditionally protected by local communities for cultural or religious reasons.
  • They conserve native biodiversity.
  • They are examples of community-based conservation.
143. Seed Bank
  • Seed banks store viable seeds for future use.
  • They preserve genetic diversity of crops and wild plants.
  • Low temperature and controlled moisture can extend seed survival.
144. Gene Bank
  • Gene banks preserve genetic material.
  • Materials can include seeds, tissues, sperm, ova or DNA.
145. Cryopreservation
  • Cryopreservation preserves biological material at extremely low temperatures.
  • Liquid nitrogen at about −196°C is commonly used.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cryopreservation → Liquid Nitrogen → −196°C

146. IUCN
  • IUCN stands for International Union for Conservation of Nature.
  • It was founded in 1948.
  • The IUCN Red List evaluates extinction risk of species.
147. IUCN Red List Categories

Major categories include:

  • NE → Not Evaluated.
  • DD → Data Deficient.
  • LC → Least Concern.
  • NT → Near Threatened.
  • VU → Vulnerable.
  • EN → Endangered.
  • CR → Critically Endangered.
  • EW → Extinct in the Wild.
  • EX → Extinct.
📌 Must-Memorise

Threatened Categories → VU + EN + CR

148. Critically Endangered
  • Critically Endangered indicates an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild.
  • It is a more severe risk category than Endangered or Vulnerable.
149. Pollution
  • Pollution is undesirable alteration of environmental quality.
  • Major forms include air, water, soil, noise, thermal and radioactive pollution.
150. Air Pollution

Important air pollutants include:

  • Particulate matter
  • Sulfur dioxide
  • Nitrogen oxides
  • Carbon monoxide
  • Ground-level ozone
  • Volatile organic compounds
  • Lead
151. Primary Pollutant
  • A primary pollutant is emitted directly from a source.

152. Secondary Pollutant
  • Secondary pollutants form through atmospheric reactions.
  • Ground-level ozone and many components of photochemical smog are secondary pollutants.

  • PM10 consists of particles with aerodynamic diameter around 10 micrometres or smaller.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

  • Carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless.
  • It results mainly from incomplete combustion.
  • It binds strongly to haemoglobin.
  • This reduces oxygen transport.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

155. Sulfur Dioxide
  • SO₂ is produced by burning sulfur-containing fuels.
  • It irritates the respiratory tract.
  • It contributes to acid rain.

  • NOₓ forms during high-temperature combustion.
  • It contributes to photochemical smog.
  • It also contributes to acid deposition.
157. Acid Rain
  • Acid rain is precipitation made unusually acidic mainly by sulfuric and nitric acids.

  • Acidifies lakes and soils.
  • Damages vegetation.
  • Mobilises toxic metals.
  • Corrodes buildings and monuments.

159. Smog

Two classic types are:

  • Classical/London smog
  • Photochemical/Los Angeles smog
160. Classical Smog
  • Classical smog is associated with smoke, sulfur pollution and fog.
  • It occurs particularly under cool, humid conditions.
  • It is sometimes called reducing smog.
161. Photochemical Smog
  • Photochemical smog develops when NOₓ and VOCs react in sunlight.
  • Important products include ground-level ozone and PAN.
  • It is favoured by sunny urban conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Photochemical Smog → NOₓ + VOC + Sunlight

162. PAN
  • PAN stands for Peroxyacetyl Nitrate.
  • It is a secondary pollutant associated with photochemical smog.
  • It irritates eyes and damages plants.
163. Water Pollution

Important sources include:

  • Domestic sewage
  • Industrial effluents
  • Agricultural runoff
  • Oil spills
  • Plastics
  • Heavy metals
164. BOD
  • BOD stands for Biochemical Oxygen Demand.
  • It measures oxygen consumed by microorganisms while decomposing biodegradable organic matter in water.
  • High BOD usually indicates high organic pollution.
📌 Must-Memorise

High BOD → More Organic Pollution → Lower Available Oxygen

165. COD
  • COD stands for Chemical Oxygen Demand.
  • It measures oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise substances in water.
  • COD generally includes a broader range of oxidisable matter than BOD.
166. Dissolved Oxygen
  • DO stands for Dissolved Oxygen.
  • Aquatic animals depend on dissolved oxygen.
  • Severe organic pollution can lower DO and cause fish deaths.
🔗 TNPSC Link

High BOD → DO ↓

167. Eutrophication
  • Eutrophication is excessive nutrient enrichment of water.
  • Nitrogen and phosphorus are major contributors.
  • Algal blooms may develop.
  • Decomposition can reduce dissolved oxygen.
📌 Must-Memorise

N + P Enrichment → Eutrophication

168. Cultural Eutrophication
  • Human activities accelerate eutrophication through fertiliser runoff, sewage and nutrient discharge.
  • This accelerated process is called cultural eutrophication.
169. Biomagnification
  • Biomagnification is increasing concentration of a persistent pollutant at successive trophic levels.
  • Top predators generally accumulate the highest concentrations.
  • DDT and methylmercury are classic examples.
📌 Must-Memorise

Biomagnification → Concentration ↑ Up Food Chain

170. Bioaccumulation
  • Bioaccumulation is buildup of a chemical within an individual organism over time.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bioaccumulation → One organism.

Biomagnification → Across trophic levels.

  • Minamata disease is severe methylmercury poisoning.
  • It became famous through industrial mercury pollution in Minamata, Japan.
  • It primarily damages the nervous system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Minamata Disease → Mercury

172. Itai-Itai Disease
  • Itai-itai disease is associated with chronic cadmium poisoning.
  • It became famous in Japan.

Itai-Itai → Cadmium

173. Lead Pollution
  • Lead is a toxic heavy metal.
  • It particularly harms the developing nervous system of children.
  • Lead exposure can also cause anaemia and kidney damage.
174. Soil Pollution

Major causes include:

  • Excess pesticides
  • Industrial waste
  • Heavy metals
  • Improper solid-waste disposal
  • Oil contamination
  • Excessive salts
175. Noise Pollution
  • Noise is unwanted or harmful sound.
  • Sound level is measured in decibels.
  • Prolonged loud noise can cause hearing loss.
  • Noise also contributes to sleep disturbance and stress.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Noise Unit → Decibel

176. Thermal Pollution
  • Thermal pollution is harmful change in natural water temperature.
  • Discharge of heated industrial or power-plant water can warm water bodies.
  • Warmer water generally holds less dissolved oxygen.
177. Radioactive Pollution
  • Radioactive contamination can arise from nuclear accidents, improper waste disposal or other sources.
  • Ionising radiation can damage DNA.
  • Radioactive materials must be isolated safely for appropriate periods.
178. Solid Waste

Important categories include:

  • Municipal waste
  • Plastic waste
  • Biomedical waste
  • Hazardous waste
  • Electronic waste
179. Waste-Management 3R
  • Reduce.
  • Reuse.
  • Recycle.
📌 Must-Memorise

Preferred First Step → Reduce Waste Generation

180. Composting
  • Composting converts biodegradable organic waste into useful soil amendment.
  • Microorganisms perform decomposition.
181. E-Waste
  • E-waste is discarded electrical and electronic equipment.
  • It can contain useful metals and hazardous substances.
  • Informal unsafe recycling can expose workers to lead, mercury and other toxins.
182. Plastic Pollution
  • Many conventional plastics degrade extremely slowly.
  • Plastic debris harms terrestrial and marine organisms.
  • Large plastics break into smaller particles called microplastics.
183. Microplastics
  • Microplastics are small plastic particles.
  • They arise from breakdown of larger plastics or are manufactured at small size.
  • They are now found widely in aquatic and terrestrial environments.
184. Greenhouse Effect
  • The greenhouse effect is a natural warming process.
  • Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation.
  • Without the natural greenhouse effect, Earth would be much colder.
  • Human activities are strengthening this effect.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Enhanced greenhouse effect drives modern global warming.

185. Major Greenhouse Gases

Important greenhouse gases include:

  • Water vapour
  • Carbon dioxide
  • Methane
  • Nitrous oxide
  • Ozone
  • Fluorinated gases
186. Carbon Dioxide

Major human sources include:

  • Fossil-fuel burning.
  • Cement production.
  • Deforestation and land-use change.
  • CO₂ is the dominant long-lived greenhouse gas emitted by human activities.
187. Methane
  • Methane formula → CH₄.
  • Sources include wetlands, livestock, rice fields, landfills and fossil-fuel systems.
  • Methane is a stronger greenhouse gas molecule-for-molecule than CO₂ over shorter timescales, though it has a shorter atmospheric lifetime.
188. Nitrous Oxide
  • N₂O is a greenhouse gas.
  • Agriculture is an important human source.
  • Nitrogen fertilisers contribute to N₂O emissions through soil microbial processes.
189. Global Warming
  • Global warming is the long-term rise in Earth's average surface temperature.
  • The principal modern cause is increased greenhouse gases from human activities.
190. Climate Change
  • Climate change includes long-term changes in temperature, rainfall, sea level, extremes and other climate characteristics.
  • Global warming is one component of climate change.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Global Warming ≠ Entire Climate Change Concept.

191. Effects of Climate Change

Major effects include:

  • Rising temperatures.
  • Melting glaciers and ice sheets.
  • Sea-level rise.
  • Changes in rainfall.
  • More severe heat extremes.
  • Ecosystem shifts.
  • Ocean warming.
  • Coral bleaching.
192. Sea-Level Rise

Major causes include:

  • Thermal expansion of warming seawater.
  • Melting of land-based glaciers.
  • Loss of ice sheets.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

193. Albedo
  • Albedo is the fraction of incoming radiation reflected by a surface.
  • Snow and ice have high albedo.
  • Dark ocean or land has lower albedo.
  • Melting ice reduces albedo and can amplify warming.
194. Ocean Acidification
  • Oceans absorb atmospheric CO₂.
  • CO₂ reacts with water to form carbonic acid.
  • Ocean pH decreases.
  • Shell-forming organisms can be affected.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

CO₂ ↑ → Ocean pH ↓

195. Carbon Footprint
  • Carbon footprint is the total greenhouse-gas emissions attributable to an activity, individual, product or organisation.
  • It is often expressed as carbon-dioxide equivalent.
196. Mitigation
  • Climate mitigation means reducing greenhouse-gas emissions or increasing carbon sinks.
  • Examples include renewable energy, energy efficiency and reforestation.
197. Adaptation
  • Climate adaptation means adjusting human or natural systems to actual or expected climate impacts.
  • Examples include drought-resistant crops, flood protection and heat-action plans.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mitigation → Reduce Cause.

Adaptation → Manage Effects.

198. Ozone Layer
  • Ozone formula is O₃.

  • It absorbs much harmful ultraviolet radiation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stratospheric Ozone → Beneficial

Tropospheric Ozone → Pollutant

199. Ozone Depletion
  • Chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting substances release chlorine or bromine radicals in the stratosphere.
  • These radicals catalytically destroy ozone.
  • Ozone depletion increases UV-B reaching Earth's surface.
200. Effects of Increased UV-B

Possible effects include:

  • Skin cancer.
  • Cataracts.
  • Immune-system effects.
  • Damage to crops and phytoplankton.
201. Ozone Hole
  • Severe seasonal ozone depletion occurs particularly over Antarctica.
  • The Antarctic ozone hole develops mainly during Southern Hemisphere spring.
  • Polar stratospheric clouds contribute to the chemistry.

  • Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer was adopted in 1985.

  • Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
  • It seeks balance among environmental, economic and social objectives.
